idiom_name: immutable shared value + keyed factory pool + extrinsic parameters
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: split the object's state into an immutable intrinsic part (the fields that are identical across a whole family of logical objects) and an extrinsic part (position, identity, request data, per-context values). Store the intrinsic part in a value that is never mutated after construction and make a factory/pool the only way to obtain it, keyed by the intrinsic state; the factory returns the existing canonical instance or creates and registers a new one. Keep the extrinsic state in a separate context object, or compute it at call time, and pass it into the shared object's operations so that one instance serves many contexts. Choose the pool's lifetime policy deliberately - process-lifetime interning, reference-counted, weak-reference-based or arena-based - and document it because the choice has correctness and security implications.
code_sketch:
canonical = pool.find(intrinsic_key)               # FlyweightFactory
if canonical is null:
    canonical = new Immutable(intrinsic_state)     # built once, never mutated
    pool.insert(intrinsic_key, canonical)
context = { shared: canonical, x, y }              # extrinsic state per object
canonical.operation(context.x, context.y)           # extrinsic state passed in
pitfalls: Splitting the state wrongly: leaving part of the context-dependent state inside the shared object either destroys the sharing (the key explodes) or corrupts unrelated contexts when it is written.
Skipping the factory: direct construction gives equal-but-distinct instances, so identity assertions and the memory saving both evaporate without any error.
Publishing a mutable shared instance - a getter returning an internal collection, or a setter left on the type - turns one write into a global corruption.
Unbounded pool growth: feeding attacker-controlled or high-cardinality keys (user names, request IDs, payload fragments) into the pool causes memory exhaustion and denial of service.
Using raw pointers that dangle after pool destruction; prefer shared_ptr, weak_ptr or arena-allocated handles with documented lifetime contracts.
Forgetting that two equal flyweight references are the same object: storing per-instance auxiliary data keyed by flyweight identity merges what should stay distinct.
